questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
These are my general reflections upon my stay in Boston.

Graduate courses in the US are typically specialized and at a high level, and I wanted to try that. BU has an impressive array of courses available to me as a student of English. Generally, BU is strong when it comes to the humanities; they do not deprioritize it in any way. I have found that at KU, the courses offered have often not been so tangibly useful or CV-oriented. The courses I took at BU are future-oriented; I did media writing, copyediting, and marketing communications. I have not been able to find that at KU. I should stress that the workload over here (including assignments and testing) throughout the semester is intense, but you get used to it. And given the hands-on nature of the courses, I get to really finetune my writing skills by producing my own original copy, receiving loads of feedback from instructors (they have SO much time for their students), editing my own texts, and editing other peoples' texts. I have one professor over here who keeps mentioning how her previous students have gotten jobs because of their endorsed copyediting skills that they got in her copyediting class.

I also wanted to experience the romance of the New England foliage which definitely lived up to my expectations; never have I seen brighter red, orange, and yellow leaves light up a city than during these past months.

I also want to stress what it means to be with people who come from backgrounds that are different from my own. I find it refreshing to have the Danish common denominator removed in social interactions; when the layer of pre-agreed opinions is not there, conversations move in a way that allows more people to be comfortable and partake freely. I want to work with producing communication. You cannot write a good text if you don't know to whom you are writing. This fall, I have gotten to cooperate and spend my time with people from Italy, Switzerland, Taiwan, India, the US, Britain, Pakistan, France, Brazil, China, etc. The multinational dynamic I have experienced feels healthy, and it has been highly rewarding both academically, professionally, and personally.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No cooking facilities for dorm-style housing where I lived. There were several meal plans to choose from (mandatory when you stay at a dorm).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The condition of BU dorms is poor to say the least, especially considering the price level. Every time I told someone I was at Warren (Warren Towers is a dorm at BU), they would say things like "I am sorry to hear that." However, it is fine for a semester, and I suppose it motivated me even more to get out of my room.

questions.answer: You can sign up for courses when you meet the prerequisites. You might contact the course instructor for approval to attend their course, or you might fill out a form and send it to the study abroad orientation manager at BU. You can also go on the waitlist if the class is full.

How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I don't think the academic level was super high. However, the immense workload makes up for that. I learned SO much because I had to be super active in class and between classes.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I don't think the academic level was super high. However, the immense workload makes up for that. I learned SO much because I had to be super active in class and between classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At BU, I had lots of class presentations, minor assignments, homework to be handed in, and occasional quizzes. At KU, I am more so used to one big exam by the end of the semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Basic Media Writing
Copyediting Fundamentals
Marketing Communication

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all three courses I took to any student who wants to improve their communication skills. I have worked in depth with so many aspects and layers of text and other modes of communication.

questions.answer: BU has about 450 different student clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the museums, parks, and cinemas. Visit all the areas of the city several times (Cambridge, Brookline, Beacon Hill, Downtown, Somerville, Allston, Seaport).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Salem or New York.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was okay, but I definitely had culture chocks more than once.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Keep an open mind; radiate that you are curious.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I wouldn't say I found anything super challenging regarding cultural differences. However, could get a bit impatient at times because the tempo is not as high as I'm used to in Copenhagen. I have to wait a long time for the elevator, and people walk and bike pretty slowly. They also make you swipe your BU ID card a lot which made me feel a bit like I could not move as freely sa I like to. I didn't feel as independent there as I do in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How kind and willing people were to help me. And politeness.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
See the different parts of Boston.
Eat lobster.
Do not stay with only people from your home institution/country.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I cannot think of anything else.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Either having met so many different people or how I was able to take 4 months out of my life in Copenhagen and create something super meaningful in Boston. I think my life at home is better now because of my time in Boston.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Loneliness at times or the responsibility creating something valuable and comfortable for yourself.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No
